title: Information System (IS)
content:
Chapter 1: Information System (IS)

Lesson 1: Introduction to Information Systems

Definition: An information system is a set of integrated elements or components that collect, manipulate and disseminate information and provide a feedback mechanism to meet an objective. The minimal IS consists of people, procedures and data.

A CBIS (Computer-Based Information System) uses computer technology as the main component. Examples include: computerised library management, hospital management, school management, and reservation systems.

Components of an Information System

  • Data and Information: Data = raw facts and figures. Information = processed data that has meaning.
  • Hardware: Physical technology – from smartphones to supercomputers.
  • Software: Programs that instruct the hardware what to do.
  • Networks: Allow computers to share resources (wired or wireless).
  • Databases: Organised collections of data for storage, accessibility and retrieval.
  • Procedures: Commands for combining components to process information.
  • People (Users): Operate hardware and create/use software.

Advantages of CBIS

  • Many users can access information simultaneously through a network.
  • Large storage capacity replaces filing cabinets.
  • Saves time, resources and money by processing information automatically.
  • Provides fast and accurate information to support decision-making.
  • Improves productivity and reduces duplication of information.

Disadvantages of CBIS

  • Security is needed to protect data.
  • Users must be trained to use the system.
  • Computers hold personal information which may be misused.
  • Expensive to develop.
  • System crashes can cause data loss.

Levels of Management in an Organisation

LevelNameRoleInformation System
TopStrategic ManagementOverall direction, long-term goalsEIS
MiddleTactical ManagementDevelop strategies and objectivesMIS / DSS
LowerOperational ManagementDay-to-day operationsTPS

Lesson 2: Types of Information Systems

1. Transaction Processing System (TPS)

Operated by shop floor workers. Provides key data to support management. Examples: payroll, order processing, reservation systems, stock control.

Characteristics: Produces information for other systems; used by operational/supervisory levels; efficiency-oriented.

2. Management Information System (MIS)

Used by middle managers to ensure smooth running of the organisation. Examples: sales management, inventory control, budgeting, personnel systems.

Characteristics: Supports structured decisions; deals with past and present; used by lower and middle management.

3. Decision Support System (DSS)

Knowledge-based system used by senior managers to project effects of decisions. Examples: logistics systems, financial planning systems.

Characteristics: Supports semi-structured decisions; has analytical/modelling capacity; concerned with predicting the future.

4. Executive Information System (EIS)

Strategic-level IS at the top of the pyramid. Helps executives analyse trends and plan long-term actions.

Characteristics: Ease of use; highly flexible; supports unstructured decisions; uses internal and external data sources; used only at senior management level.

title: Modelling and Simulation
content:
Chapter 2: Modelling and Simulating Systems

1. Modelling Systems

System modelling is the process of using models to conceptualise and construct systems in business and IT development.

A model is a precise representation of how a system works. It can also be an abstract representation of an object or set of objects having common characteristics.

2. Simulation Systems

A simulation system is a system that imitates the real system to find out what happens under different situations and conditions. It involves creating models and then testing how they behave.

Simulations avoid the expense or danger of making mistakes in the real system. Examples: traffic simulation, flight simulators, pilot training.

3. Advantages of Modelling and Simulation

  • Safer and cheaper than real-world testing.
  • Able to test a product or system before building it.
  • Can identify unexpected problems early.
  • Able to explore 'what if…' questions.
  • Can speed things up or slow them down to see changes over long or short periods.

4. Disadvantages of Modelling and Simulation

  • Mistakes may be made in programming the simulation.
  • Cost of the simulation model can be high.
  • Running several simulations may be expensive.
  • Time may be needed to interpret the results.
  • People's reactions in the simulation might not be realistic.

5. What-If Analysis Using Spreadsheet (MS Excel)

What-if analysis is the process of changing values in cells to see how those changes affect the outcome of formulas on the worksheet.

Three kinds of What-If Analysis tools in Excel:

  • Scenarios: Save and switch between sets of input values.
  • Goal Seek: Specify a target result and find the input value needed.
  • Data Tables: Work with one or two variables to explore many possible results.

title: Monitoring and Control Systems
content:
Chapter 3: Monitoring and Control Systems

1. Monitoring Systems

A monitoring system collects and reports data about the state of a system without making changes to it. It only observes and reports.

Examples: weather monitoring stations, hospital patient monitoring, CCTV systems, environmental sensors.

Components: Sensors (collect data) → Processor (analyses data) → Output device (displays results).

2. Control Systems

A control system not only monitors but also takes automatic action to adjust the system based on feedback. It uses a feedback loop.

Examples: central heating thermostat, automatic traffic lights, autopilot in aircraft, industrial robots.

Components: Sensors → Processor → Actuators (make changes to the system).

3. Difference Between Monitoring and Control Systems

FeatureMonitoring SystemControl System
Action takenObserves and reports onlyObserves AND makes adjustments
Feedback loopNo feedback loopUses feedback loop
Human requiredHuman makes decisionsCan operate autonomously
ExampleWeather stationCentral heating thermostat

title: System Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
content:
Chapter 4: System Development Life Cycle (SDLC)

SDLC is a structured process used to develop information systems. It provides a systematic approach to planning, creating, testing, and delivering an information system.

Stages of the SDLC

1. Planning / Investigation Phase

The feasibility of the project is assessed. A preliminary study is done to determine whether the project is viable (technically, financially, operationally). A project scope and plan are created.

2. Analysis Phase

Requirements are gathered from users and stakeholders. The current system is analysed to identify problems. A requirements specification document is produced.

3. Design Phase

The system design is created – including database design, user interface design, and process design. Hardware and software requirements are specified.

4. Development (Implementation/Coding) Phase

The actual system is built/coded based on the design. Programmers write code, databases are created, and hardware is installed.

5. Testing Phase

The system is thoroughly tested to find and fix errors. Types of testing: unit testing, integration testing, system testing, user acceptance testing (UAT).

6. Implementation Phase

The new system is deployed to users. Changeover strategies:

  • Direct/Plunge: Old system switched off, new one switches on immediately. Risky but cheap.
  • Parallel: Both old and new systems run simultaneously for a period. Safe but expensive.
  • Pilot: New system tested with a small group of selected users before full rollout.
  • Phased: New system introduced gradually, one part at a time.

7. Maintenance Phase

The system is monitored and updated after deployment. Includes fixing bugs, improving performance, and adapting to new needs.

SDLC Models

  • Waterfall Model: Linear, sequential. Each phase must be completed before the next begins.
  • Agile Model: Iterative, flexible. Work done in short cycles (sprints).
  • Spiral Model: Combines iterative development with risk analysis.
  • Rapid Application Development (RAD): Focuses on quick prototyping and user feedback.

title: Data Capture and Outsourcing
content:
Chapter 5: Data Capture and Outsourcing

1. Data Capture

Data capture is the process of collecting data and entering it into a computer system.

Manual Data Capture Methods

  • Keyboard entry: Typing data directly.
  • Mouse/touchscreen: Clicking/tapping to input.
  • Voice input: Speaking into a microphone.

Automated Data Capture Methods

  • OMR (Optical Mark Recognition): Reads marks made on paper (e.g., answer sheets).
  • OCR (Optical Character Recognition): Reads printed/handwritten text.
  • MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition): Reads characters printed in magnetic ink (e.g., bank cheques).
  • Barcode reader: Reads barcodes on products.
  • QR code reader: Reads 2D QR codes.
  • RFID (Radio Frequency Identification): Reads radio signals from tags.
  • Biometrics: Fingerprints, iris scan, face recognition.

Data Verification vs. Data Validation

FeatureVerificationValidation
DefinitionChecking data is correctly transferredChecking data is sensible/reasonable
Done byHuman or double-entry checkComputer (rules set by programmer)
ExampleTyping a password twiceAge must be between 0 and 120

Validation Checks

  • Range check: Value must be within a defined range (e.g., age 1–120).
  • Type check: Data must be the correct type (e.g., numbers only).
  • Presence check: Field must not be empty.
  • Length check: Data must be a specific length.
  • Format check: Data must match a pattern (e.g., date format DD/MM/YYYY).
  • Lookup check: Value must match an entry in a list.

2. Outsourcing

Outsourcing is the practice of a business hiring an external company or individual to perform services or create goods that traditionally were performed in-house.

Advantages: Cost savings, access to specialised skills, focus on core business, flexibility.

Disadvantages: Loss of control, security risks, communication difficulties, dependency on external provider.

title: Database and Data Resource Management
content:
Chapter 6: Database and Data Resource Management

Key Definitions

Data: Raw facts and figures with no meaning on their own (e.g., 25, "John").
Information: Data that has been processed to give it meaning (e.g., John is 25 years old).
Database: An organised collection of structured data, typically stored electronically and managed by a DBMS.

Database Terminology

TermDefinitionExample
Field (Attribute)A single piece of data about an entityName, Age, StudentID
RecordA collection of related fieldsOne student's complete entry
Table (Relation)A collection of related recordsStudents table
Primary KeyA field that uniquely identifies each recordStudentID
Foreign KeyA field that links one table to the primary key of anotherClassID in Student table

Types of Databases

  • Flat File Database: Single table, no relationships. Simple but prone to redundancy.
  • Relational Database: Multiple tables linked by keys. Reduces redundancy. Most common type.
  • Object-Oriented Database: Stores data as objects.
  • Distributed Database: Data stored across multiple locations.

Normalisation

Normalisation is the process of organising data in a database to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity.

  • 1NF (First Normal Form): No repeating groups; all attributes are atomic (single values).
  • 2NF (Second Normal Form): In 1NF + no partial dependencies (every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key).
  • 3NF (Third Normal Form): In 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key attributes depend only on the primary key).

DBMS (Database Management System)

A DBMS is software that manages and organises databases. Examples: Microsoft Access, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL.

Features of a DBMS

  • Data storage and retrieval
  • Data security and access control
  • Data integrity enforcement
  • Backup and recovery
  • Query processing (using SQL)

Data Integrity

Data integrity refers to the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of data throughout its lifecycle.

Ways to ensure data integrity: validation checks, access controls, transaction management, regular backups, encryption.

title: Project Management
content:
Chapter 9: Project Management

A project is a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. It has a defined beginning and end.

Key Definitions

  • Project Management: Planning, scheduling, and controlling activities to achieve project objectives within constraints of time, cost, and quality.
  • Project Manager: Person responsible for leading the project team and ensuring project goals are met.
  • Milestone: A significant point or event in the project (no duration).
  • Critical Path: The longest sequence of tasks that determines the minimum project duration.
  • Slack Time (Float): The amount of time a task can be delayed without delaying the overall project.
  • Task/Activity: A specific piece of work with a duration.

Project Life Cycle

  1. Initiation: Define the project goal and feasibility.
  2. Planning: Create a detailed plan, schedule, and budget.
  3. Execution: Carry out the project plan.
  4. Monitoring & Control: Track progress against the plan.
  5. Closure: Deliver the final product and review the project.

Project Management Tools

Gantt Chart

A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar chart that shows the schedule of project activities over time. Each bar represents a task and shows its start date, duration, and end date.

Advantages: Easy to understand, shows task duration and overlap, easy to update.

Disadvantages: Does not show dependencies between tasks clearly, can become complex for large projects.

PERT Chart (Program Evaluation and Review Technique)

A PERT chart is a network diagram showing the sequence and dependencies of project tasks. It is used to identify the critical path.

Key Terms:

  • Early Start (ES): Earliest a task can start.
  • Early Finish (EF): Earliest a task can finish = ES + Duration.
  • Late Start (LS): Latest a task can start without delaying project.
  • Late Finish (LF): Latest a task can finish without delaying project.
  • Slack = LS – ES (or LF – EF)
Critical Path: The path through the PERT chart where all tasks have zero slack. This is the longest path and determines the project duration.

Difference: Gantt Chart vs PERT Chart

FeatureGantt ChartPERT Chart
FormatBar chartNetwork diagram
Shows dependenciesNot clearlyYes, clearly
Shows critical pathNoYes
Ease of understandingEasyMore complex
